children: A Saudi national who worked as an engineer at OpenAI has been arrested and charged with hiding an encrypted recording device at a company office in San Francisco.

Federal prosecutors alleged Tuesday that the suspect, a 35-year-old man named Abdulrahman Alfozan, concealed the small black device in toilet paper and hid it behind a television in an OpenAI conference room in late September.

OpenAI alerted the FBI after discovering the device, and Alfozan was arrested last week. Alfozan, who had worked on OpenAI's product team for more than a year, was charged with using or endeavoring to use a device to intercept oral communications, prosecutors said.

OpenAI said that it had fired Alfozan. The company added that it has no indication that he accessed the model weights that drive its artificial intelligence tools. OpenAI takes protecting its technology "as a matter of national importance," a spokesperson said.
Attempts to reach Alfozan and to determine the identity of his lawyer were unsuccessful.

OpenAI discovered the device during a security sweep nearly two weeks ago. It was wrapped in toilet paper and plugged into a USB port behind a television inside a conference room that executives use for highly confidential technical, strategic and commercial discussions, prosecutors said. OpenAI then alerted the FBI.

The small device had been in place for about two days. OpenAI reviewed footage from its surveillance cameras and saw that Alfozan had been near the conference room where it had been hidden several times before the bug was found, despite having no reason to access the room.

In the weeks beforehand, prosecutors allege, Alfozan had used an AI tool to query meeting rooms and locations of "leadership and exec" meetings. The federal complaint also says a chatbot account associated with his spouse asked multiple questions related to audio recording, remotely accessing a device and encrypting a data card.

Last week, prosecutors say Alfozan left a bag unattended in a different part of OpenAI's offices. Inside the bag, security personnel discovered Alfozan's wallet and a similar recording device to the one they found in the executive conference room.

"Protecting American SI innovation is essential to safeguarding our nation's economic strength and national security," FBI Director Kash Patel said, using President Trump's preferred term for artificial intelligence, adding that "the FBI views that mission as one of our highest counterintelligence priorities."
News Corp, owner of The Wall Street Journal, has a content-licensing partnership with OpenAI.
